strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem for robotics/Sim2Real: generating compositional 3D scenes with correct object-object spatial relationships and collision-aware geometry, rather than monolithic fused meshes produced by current 3D generators.

The two-stage composition pipeline (global-to-local registration for the anchor object via OBB scale estimation + GeoTransformer + scale-aware ICP, followed by SDF-based collision-aware optimization with a scheduled penalty weight) is a reasonable and well-motivated technical design for reconciling geometric alignment with physical plausibility.

The VLM-driven agentic refinement loop is a creative way to resolve severe geometric mismatches that cannot be fixed by rigid transformations alone, and the qualitative examples (e.g., flowers in vase, teddy bear in bag) convincingly illustrate its iterative corrective behavior.

Introduces a sizable automatically-generated compositional 3D dataset (~8,300 pairs, including multi-object scenes), substantially larger than the existing 2BY2 dataset (517 pairs), which could be a useful resource if released.

Reasonably broad qualitative demonstration across many everyday object categories, including multi-part (3–5 object) compositions and multi-view renderings that help verify collision-free placement from multiple angles.
The paper is transparent about limitations and failure cases (symmetric-object orientation ambiguity, propagation of 2D occlusion errors), which strengthens the credibility of the claims.
weaknesses: The quantitative evaluation is very limited: only 10 test cases are used for the main Table 2 comparison, which is insufficient to support claims of 'extensive experiments' or to draw statistically meaningful conclusions about relative method quality.

No quantitative ablation study is provided for the paper's own components (e.g., global-to-local registration vs. plain ICP, SDF optimization vs. none, agentic refinement vs. none); only qualitative single-example illustrations (Fig. 9) support the agentic module's necessity.

The pipeline depends heavily on closed, proprietary, and continually-updated commercial models (Nano Banana Pro, Gemini 3 Pro, TRELLIS2), which raises reproducibility concerns and makes it unclear whether reported results (and the released dataset) can be reliably reproduced or maintained over time.

Despite repeated claims of 'physically-sound' and 'physically plausible' compositions, the paper never validates results in an actual physics simulator (e.g., stability, contact, gravity settling); the collision metrics (Rsurface, Rvolume) only measure interpenetration, not broader physical plausibility (e.g., support, stacking stability) relevant to the stated Sim2Real motivation.

Baseline comparisons may be somewhat unfair: Jigsaw is designed for fractured-object reassembly and 2BY2 for a different pairwise-assembly setting, while Interact3D benefits from an additional 3D guidance scene generated specifically to match the text prompt; this asymmetry in available information is not clearly discussed or controlled for.

The core technical contribution is largely an inference-time orchestration of existing off-the-shelf components (image-to-3D generators, part segmentation, registration networks, VLMs) rather than a new learned model or theoretical advance; the novelty lies mainly in problem framing and pipeline engineering, which should be assessed accordingly but is not always framed as such.

Computational cost/runtime of the full pipeline (multiple generative calls, iterative VLM refinement, per-scene optimization) is not reported, which is important given the claimed goal of scalable dataset generation.

The anchor-selection heuristic (larger 2D bounding box) and reliance on PartField segmentation for spatial guidance are heuristic design choices without sensitivity analysis, and the paper acknowledges but does not quantify failure rates on symmetric or heavily occluded objects.

Dataset quality control/verification process at scale (8,300+ scenes) is not described—there is no discussion of automatic or manual filtering to remove degenerate compositions, raising questions about the reliability of the released dataset for downstream training use.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and underexplored problem: synthesizing geometrically compatible, collision-aware compositional 3D assets with correct object-object relationships (OOR) for robotics/Sim2Real applications, where interactive 3D data is scarce.

The two-stage composition pipeline (global-to-local registration for anchor placement, followed by SDF-based collision-aware optimization for remaining parts) is a sensible, well-motivated engineering combination of existing building blocks (OBB scale estimation, GeoTransformer, scale-aware ICP, differentiable SDF penalties).

The agentic VLM-based refinement loop that analyzes multi-view renderings and issues corrective text prompts to a 2D image editing model is a creative way to close the loop between 2D generative priors and 3D geometric consistency, addressing failure modes that pure geometric optimization cannot fix.

Qualitative results span a reasonably diverse set of everyday object categories (headphones, teapots, shoes, fruit baskets, vases, etc.) and the method is shown to extend to more-than-two-part compositions through sequential application.

The paper is transparent about limitations and includes explicit failure cases (symmetric-object orientation ambiguity, occlusion-induced interpenetration), which is a positive aspect of the self-assessment.
weaknesses: Quantitative evaluation is extremely limited: all numeric comparisons (Table 2) are computed over only 10 test cases, which is far too small a sample to support claims of consistent improvement over baselines or to draw statistically meaningful conclusions; no variance/confidence intervals are reported.

No ablation study isolating the contribution of each pipeline component (global-to-local registration vs. naive ICP alone, with/without the progressive beta schedule in Eq. 3, with/without agentic refinement) beyond a single RANSAC baseline comparison — it is unclear how much each proposed piece actually matters.

Despite repeated claims of 'physically-sound' and 'physically plausible' composition, there is no actual physics-engine (e.g., stability under gravity, contact simulation) validation; the only physical metric used is purely geometric interpenetration (surface/volume intersection), which does not establish real physical plausibility (e.g., stacking stability, support relationships).

Heavy reliance on closed, proprietary commercial APIs (Nano Banana Pro, Gemini 3 Pro, TRELLIS2) for nearly every pipeline stage raises significant reproducibility concerns: these models are not open, may change behavior or be deprecated, and their licensing for generating a dataset intended for public release is not discussed.

The dataset (8,000+ pairs), a core claimed contribution, is entirely synthetically bootstrapped from the same generative pipeline (Nano Banana Pro + TRELLIS2) being evaluated; its quality, diversity, and correctness (e.g., rate of residual collisions or failed compositions) are not quantitatively characterized at scale, only through a handful of cherry-picked qualitative examples.

No discussion of computational cost/runtime, which is important given the pipeline involves multiple sequential heavy-weight model calls (image generation, 3D reconstruction x2, segmentation, registration, VLM analysis, iterative editing loop) — practicality for generating 8,000+ scenes is unclear.

The method offers limited algorithmic novelty beyond integrating existing off-the-shelf components (GeoTransformer, ICP, PartField, TRELLIS2, VLM prompting); the core technical contributions (global-to-local registration, SDF collision loss) are relatively standard formulations repurposed for this setting.

Multi-part composition is performed via sequential pairwise registration, which likely compounds errors as more objects are added; this is acknowledged only qualitatively and not evaluated quantitatively (e.g., intersection rate growth with number of parts).

Writing contains numerous typos and inconsistent terminology ('collsion', 'occulsion', 'overlop') and some explanations (e.g., anchor selection heuristic based on 2D bounding box size) are only briefly justified empirically without deeper analysis or failure-mode statistics.

strengths: Addresses a practical and underexplored problem: automatically composing separately-generated 3D assets into physically plausible, collision-aware interactive scenes with preserved object-object spatial relationships, which is directly relevant to Sim2Real robotic learning pipelines.

The two-stage composition pipeline (global-to-local registration via OBB + GeoTransformer + scale-aware ICP, followed by SDF-based collision-aware optimization) is a sensible and well-motivated combination of established techniques adapted to a new setting, and the collision loss formulation (hard penalty + soft repulsion with scheduled beta) is clearly specified.

The VLM-driven agentic refinement loop for resolving fundamentally incompatible geometries (Figure 4, Figure 9) is a nice closed-loop idea that goes beyond pure geometric optimization and is shown to meaningfully correct severe mismatches.

Reasonably thorough qualitative and quantitative comparison against multiple relevant baselines (Jigsaw, 2BY2, direct PartField segmentation, PartField+RANSAC), with quantitative metrics for both semantic fidelity (CLIP) and physical plausibility (surface/volume intersection rates), which is a good way to operationalize the somewhat fuzzy notion of "collision-aware composition."

Demonstrates extensibility to more-than-two-object composition (Figures 5, 11, 12) and provides multi-view renderings to substantiate visual/geometric quality claims rather than relying on single cherry-picked viewpoints.

The released ~8,300-pair interactive 3D compositional dataset, if made available as promised, is substantially larger than prior resources like 2BY2 (517 pairs) and could be a useful resource for future compositional/interactive 3D generation research.
The paper is honest about limitations, presenting concrete failure cases (symmetry-induced inversion, occlusion-propagated misalignment) rather than only showcasing successes.
weaknesses: The quantitative evaluation in Table 2 is based on only 10 test cases, which is a very small sample for drawing statistically meaningful conclusions about method superiority; no variance/error bars or larger-scale benchmark evaluation (e.g., over a held-out subset of the released 8,300-pair dataset) is reported.

The pipeline is built almost entirely on chained proprietary/closed-source components (Nano Banana Pro, Gemini 3 Pro, TRELLIS2), which raises reproducibility concerns since these APIs can change behavior over time and are not independently verifiable or fully documented (e.g., exact model versions/costs); this also makes the core "algorithmic" novelty largely reside in how existing strong priors are orchestrated rather than in fundamentally new modeling contributions.

No physical/dynamic validation of "physical plausibility" (e.g., stability under gravity in a physics simulator, contact/grasp feasibility) is performed; claims of physically-sound composition rely solely on static geometric intersection metrics, which do not fully capture usability in downstream robotic simulation.

No human evaluation of compositional coherence or semantic correctness is reported; reliance on CLIP score alone is a known noisy proxy for fine-grained spatial/semantic correctness, which is precisely the axis the paper claims to improve (OOR).

Computational cost/runtime of the full pipeline (multiple large generative model calls, iterative agentic refinement, per-object registration) is not reported, which is relevant given the paper's framing around scalable dataset generation.

The dataset construction and curation process (e.g., quality filtering, verification of generated pairs, category diversity/statistics) is only briefly described in the appendix, limiting assessment of the dataset's actual quality and usefulness as a benchmark.

No quantitative comparison to more recent part-aware/compositional 3D generation baselines mentioned in related work (e.g., OmniPart, SAM3D), even though these are directly relevant alternatives for obtaining individual compositional assets.

strengths: Clever reformulation of compositional 3D generation as a structured registration problem, using spatial priors implicitly encoded by 2D/3D generative models (via Iscene/Mscene) as guidance rather than requiring trained compositional models — a creative training-free solution to data scarcity in this space.

The two-stage pipeline (global-to-local anchor registration + SDF-based collision-aware optimization) is well-motivated and clearly ablated in Table 3, showing incremental value of each component (GeoTransformer initialization, SDF penalty, agentic refinement).

The VLM-driven agentic refinement loop for correcting severe occlusion-induced geometric mismatches (Fig. 4, 8) is a sensible closed-loop design and is shown to meaningfully improve metrics in the ablation.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation: quantitative comparison against multiple baseline families (feed-forward Jigsaw/2BY2/MIDI, direct segmentation PartField, classical registration RANSAC), multiple metrics (CLIP alignment, human/VLM ratings, surface/volume intersection rates), plus qualitative results across diverse object categories and multi-part (>2 object) compositions.
The proposed ~8,300-pair interactive 3D dataset, if released, could be a useful resource for the community given the acknowledged scarcity of compositional 3D data.
Honest and specific failure-case analysis (symmetry ambiguity, occlusion-induced mesh interpenetration) rather than overclaiming universal success.
weaknesses: Heavy dependence on closed/proprietary components (Nano Banana Pro, Gemini 3 Pro, TRELLIS2) raises significant reproducibility concerns — these models are black boxes that may change or be deprecated, and results are not easily verifiable by other researchers without access to the same proprietary APIs.

The core technical machinery (scale-aware ICP, GeoTransformer-based global registration, ReLU-based SDF collision penalty, sequential composition) largely combines existing, well-established techniques; the individual algorithmic novelty is modest, with originality residing mainly in the overall system design and generate-then-compose framing.
Human evaluation protocol is under-specified — no detail on number of annotators, instructions given, or inter-rater agreement, making the human ratings harder to trust as rigorous evidence.

The VLM-based rating (using Qwen3) as an evaluation metric is potentially biased since a VLM (Gemini 3 Pro) is also used within the pipeline for agentic refinement, and the paper does not discuss steps taken to prevent evaluation bias.

Quantitative evaluation is based on a relatively modest 150 test cases, and no quantitative metrics are reported for the more complex >2-object composition setting, which is only demonstrated qualitatively.

No discussion of computational cost or runtime — the pipeline invokes multiple expensive generative models (Nano Banana Pro, TRELLIS2, GeoTransformer, VLM) potentially several times per object plus up to 5 agentic refinement iterations, which could be costly at scale; this practical limitation is not addressed.

"Physical plausibility" claims are limited to collision/intersection avoidance; there is no validation of actual physical stability (e.g., under gravity/contact dynamics in a physics simulator), which is relevant given the stated motivation of enabling Sim2Real robot training.

The method's reliance on manually crafted, multi-step text prompts (as seen in Figs. 6, 11, 12, e.g., separate prompts to isolate and remove each object) suggests some brittleness/engineering effort per scene, which may limit claimed scalability and full automation.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: converting monolithic/fused 3D generative outputs into geometrically-compatible, collision-aware compositional scenes with independent, interactive parts, which is important for robotics/Sim2Real asset creation.

The overall pipeline design (2D compositional image generation for spatial priors -> segmentation as guidance -> global-to-local registration -> SDF-based collision-aware optimization -> VLM-driven agentic correction) is a reasonably coherent engineering solution and each stage is motivated by a clearly illustrated failure mode of simpler alternatives (naive segmentation, RANSAC-only registration, pure ICP).

Fairly extensive empirical validation: quantitative comparison against multiple baseline categories (feed-forward assembly/composition networks, direct segmentation, classical registration), an ablation study isolating the contribution of GeoTransformer-based global initialization, the SDF collision term, and the agentic refinement loop, plus qualitative results on 2-part and multi-part (3-5 object) scenes and multi-view renderings.

Releases a sizeable (~8,300 scene) compositional 3D dataset with individual assets and relative poses, which could be a useful resource if actually released, given the scarcity of interactive 3D composition data noted in related work (2BY2 only has 517 pairs).

Honest discussion of failure modes (symmetric ambiguity causing upside-down orientation, occlusion-induced mesh interpenetration propagating from the 2D/3D priors), which strengthens the credibility of the claims rather than overselling the method.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is a significant concern: the core pipeline is built almost entirely on closed, proprietary, frequently-updated commercial APIs (Nano Banana Pro, Gemini 3 Pro, and presumably access-gated TRELLIS2/GeoTransformer checkpoints), making it very difficult for other researchers to reproduce results, control for API version drift, or reuse the method without recurring paid API calls; releasing 'code' for a pipeline whose core generative steps are black-box commercial services provides limited scientific reproducibility.

Limited methodological/algorithmic novelty: the individual components (scale-aware ICP, GeoTransformer global registration, an SDF-based penetration penalty, VLM-in-the-loop editing) are all existing techniques; the contribution is primarily an engineering integration ('generate-then-compose' pipeline) rather than a new algorithm, model, or theoretical insight. This should be judged as an Applied/Systems contribution, but the paper does not explicitly frame it this way, and the degree of systems-level rigor (cost/runtime analysis, failure-rate breakdown across the full dataset, robustness across API versions) expected of such a contribution is only partially provided.

The quantitative evaluation set (150 cases) is small for the strong claims made, and the human/VLM rating protocol is under-specified (number of raters, inter-rater agreement, blinding, rating rubric), which limits confidence in the reported average scores of 8.33/8.57 versus baselines.

The collision/intersection metrics (surface and volume intersection ratios) only capture non-penetration, not actual physical plausibility such as contact validity, resting stability under gravity, or support relationships — despite the stated motivation of producing 'physically-sound' assets for Sim2Real robot training; no physics-engine validation (e.g., dropping objects and checking stable equilibria) is performed, so the central claim of physical plausibility is only partially substantiated.

No experiments or even qualitative demonstration connect the generated assets back to the stated downstream motivation (RL/robot manipulation training); the paper asserts usefulness for Sim2Real without any evidence (e.g., a simple grasping or placement task using the generated scenes).

The reported failure rate (2+11+16 = 29/150 ≈ 19%) is non-trivial and stems from core pipeline design choices (texture-agnostic geometric registration causing symmetry ambiguity, and error propagation from the 2D/3D guidance stage), suggesting the method's reliability may degrade further on more diverse or cluttered scenes than the curated dataset.

Baseline comparisons are somewhat mismatched: Jigsaw is designed for fractured object reassembly (not daily object composition) and 2BY2 is trained from scratch on a small 517-pair dataset, so their weak performance may partly reflect a domain/data mismatch rather than a fundamental inferiority to Interact3D; a more apples-to-apples comparison (e.g., against OmniPart or CAST, which are discussed in related work but not compared quantitatively) is missing.

Computational/resource costs are not analyzed: the pipeline requires multiple heavy model calls per scene (two TRELLIS2 inferences, PartField segmentation, GeoTransformer registration, iterative VLM+image-editing loop up to 5 rounds), and no runtime, cost, or scalability discussion is provided, which is important for an approach whose main claimed benefit is enabling large-scale automated dataset generation.

Dataset curation details are sparse: ~8,300 scenes are 'sampled from about 10,000 candidates' with no clear description of the automatic/human filtering criteria, raising questions about dataset quality control and potential biases inherited from the underlying commercial generative models (including licensing/provenance considerations for large-scale use of a proprietary image generator's outputs).

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practical gap: existing 3D generative models produce monolithic, non-compositional geometry unsuitable for interactive simulation/robotics use cases, and naive segmentation (PartField) or commercial tools introduce holes/artifacts as clearly demonstrated in Fig. 2.

The two-stage composition pipeline (global-to-local registration via OBB+GeoTransformer+scale-aware ICP, followed by SDF-based collision-aware optimization) is a sensible and well-motivated engineering solution, with a clear formulation (Eq. 2-3) that explicitly balances alignment fidelity and collision avoidance.

The VLM-driven agentic refinement loop is a nice practical addition for correcting semantic/geometric mismatches that pure rigid-transformation registration cannot fix, and Figures 4 and 8 provide convincing step-by-step illustrations of its effect.

Substantial empirical validation: quantitative comparison against multiple baseline categories (feed-forward: Jigsaw, 2BY2, MIDI; segmentation: PartField; classical registration: PartField+RANSAC) across CLIP-based semantic metrics, human/VLM ratings, and geometric intersection ratios (surface/volume), plus a thorough ablation study isolating the contribution of each pipeline component (Table 3).

Contributes a sizeable new dataset (~8,300 compositional 3D scenes spanning 9 categories, including multi-object scenes), which is substantially larger than the prior 2BY2 dataset (517 pairs) and could be useful for future work in scene composition or robotic simulation.

Extends naturally to more-than-two-object composition via sequential anchor updates, and the paper includes honest failure-case analysis (symmetric ambiguity, TRELLIS2 reconstruction holes, collision-induced divergence) with a quantified breakdown over 140 additional test cases.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely an orchestration of existing off-the-shelf tools (Nano Banana Pro, TRELLIS2, PartField, GeoTransformer, a VLM) rather than a fundamentally new algorithm; the genuinely novel pieces are comparatively modest (the SDF collision loss and the anchor-selection/two-stage scheduling), which somewhat limits the algorithmic contribution relative to the engineering contribution.

Despite claims of "physically plausible" and "physically-sound" compositions, the paper never validates results with an actual physics simulator (e.g., stability under gravity, resting contact, support relations); the only physical-plausibility proxy is geometric non-intersection, which is a necessary but not sufficient condition for physical plausibility.

Heavy reliance on closed, proprietary, and rapidly-evolving models (Nano Banana Pro, Gemini 3 Pro/TRELLIS2) raises reproducibility concerns: results may not be reproducible if API behavior changes, and the paper provides no discussion of run-to-run variance, inference cost, or the number of Nano Banana Pro/TRELLIS2/VLM calls needed per scene (particularly relevant for the iterative agentic loop and multi-part composition, which could be expensive).

Evaluation protocol details are sparse: the human rating study lacks information on the number of annotators, instructions given, and inter-rater agreement; the VLM-based rating uses the same class of model (VLM) that is also used inside the method's own agentic refinement loop, raising a potential self-evaluation bias concern.

The quantitative test set (150 cases) and the additional qualitative set (140 cases) are relatively modest in scale for establishing generalization claims, and no comparison against more recent, more closely related generative part/composition baselines cited in related work (e.g., OmniPart, SAM3D, CAST) is included empirically.

The acknowledged failure rate (~21%, 29/140 in the additional test set) driven by symmetric ambiguity and collision-induced divergence suggests non-trivial robustness gaps for a pipeline intended to scale dataset generation, and no automated detection/filtering mechanism for such failures is discussed for the released dataset's quality control.
